lesson.subtitle: Lesson 4 -- If You Do, We Will
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Fábia | Lesson 4 -- If You Do, We Will

listenings.text: Hi, thanks for the note. So, you would like two extra reports a month. Let me be straight with you: those are not in the current scope, but I am not going to say no. Here is what I would suggest. If we move you to a monthly retainer instead of the fixed contract, the two reports come inside it and you stop worrying about what is included. And one condition on our side: if your team sends the data by the tenth, the reports will be ready in the same month rather than the following one. If that works for you, I will follow up with a revised proposal today.

Let me ask you something. How many people do you have on this internally? Three, is that right? Two on payroll and one part-time on tax. Now, if we took the whole thing over, you would not need three. You would keep one person as our point of contact, and you would move the other two into the finance team you told me you have been trying to build for a year. That is the part people miss. It is not about cutting heads, it is about where those heads sit. I am not going to give you a number today. Go and work out what those three people cost you, all in, and then we will have a much more useful conversation.

reading.rtitle: How a contract grew by forty per cent, one favour at a time
paras: In January the contract was simple: payroll for 30 employees, one monthly report, one invoice. The client was happy and the provider was profitable.

In March the client asked for a second report. It took two hours to build, so the provider said yes and did not charge. In May they asked for the same report weekly. That was eight hours a month, still unbilled.

In July the client's head office started asking questions directly, by email, in English, at eleven at night. Someone had to answer them. By September the provider had put a second analyst on the account, and nobody had signed anything new since January.
The contract had grown by roughly forty per cent in work and zero per cent in fee. When the provider finally raised it, the client was genuinely surprised: from where they sat, nothing had changed.
Nobody acted in bad faith. Every single request, on its own, was reasonable. That is precisely what makes scope creep hard to see, and harder to talk about once it has happened.
reading.source: Composite case written for this lesson, based on a common pattern in outsourcing contracts.

a fixed point that has to be reached
work that grows past the contract
to take a problem higher up

items.situation: "Could you add two more reports? It's a small change." Protect the scope without refusing.
tips: Of course. If we add ... , we will need to ...
